title: The Pandya chief Senguttuvan visits the forest
body: The Silappadikaram, an epic written in Tamil, describes a visit by the chief Senguttuvan to the forest. People came down the mountain, singing and dancing, and, just as the defeated show respect to the victorious king, they brought gifts: ivory, fragrant wood, fans made of the hair of deer, honey, sandalwood, red ochre, antimony, turmeric, cardamom and pepper, as well as coconuts, mangoes, medicinal plants, sugarcane, flowers, areca nut, bananas, and animals and birds such as baby tigers, elephants, monkeys, deer, peacocks and speaking parrots. Chiefs, unlike kings who usually collected taxes, received gifts from their subordinates and often distributed these amongst their supporters.

title: The Sudarshana lake in Gujarat
body: A Sanskrit rock inscription at Girnar (c. second century CE), composed to record the achievements of the Shaka ruler Rudradaman, tells us about the Sudarshana (beautiful) lake, an artificial reservoir. According to the inscription, the lake, with its embankments and water channels, was built by a local governor during the rule of the Mauryas. A terrible storm later broke the embankments and water gushed out. Rudradaman, then ruling in the area, claimed to have got the lake repaired using his own resources, without imposing any tax on his subjects. Another inscription on the same rock (c. fifth century) mentions how one of the rulers of the Gupta dynasty got the lake repaired once again.

title: Prabhavati Gupta and the village of Danguna
body: Prabhavati Gupta was the daughter of Chandragupta II (c. 375-415 CE) and was married into the Vakataka ruling family of the Deccan. In her inscription she commands the gramakutumbinas (householders or peasants), Brahmanas and others living in the village of Danguna that she has donated the village, to increase her religious merit, to the Acharya Chanalasvamin, whose commands they should obey. The village receives the exemptions typical of an agrahara: it is not to be entered by soldiers and policemen; it is exempt from providing grass, hides and charcoal to touring royal officers, and from supplying flowers and milk; and it is granted with the right to hidden treasures and with major and minor taxes. According to Sanskrit legal texts, women were not supposed to have independent access to resources such as land.
